title: Early Retirement Health Insurance Options Before 65
metaDescription: Review early retirement health insurance options before Medicare at 65. Compare COBRA rules, Marketplace enrollment windows, and coverage tradeoffs.
h1: Early Retirement Health Insurance Options Before 65
cardBlurb: Review early retirement health insurance choices before age 65, including COBRA rules, Marketplace special enrollment periods, and key transition steps.
introText:
To get early retirement health insurance before Medicare, you can use COBRA continuation coverage for usually up to 18 months at up to 102% of the plan cost with 60 days to enroll, or choose a Marketplace plan during a 60-day Special Enrollment Period before or after losing job-based coverage. At ModernWallet, we treat the cost of this coverage as a line item to confirm before the rest of the plan. Coverage can also come from another employer plan if available, while Medicare eligibility begins at age 65.

You must replace group medical benefits if you leave an employer before Medicare enrollment begins three months before the month you turn 65. Clear election windows, premium obligations, and enrollment requirements help you secure coverage without coverage gaps.

sections.heading: Early Retirement Health Insurance Options Before Medicare
sections.body:
Early retirement health insurance covers the gap between leaving work and reaching Medicare eligibility at age 65. The Medicare Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) begins three months before the month you turn 65, as stated on [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start). Coverage start after IEP enrollment depends on the month you enroll.

Retiring before age 65 creates a period where you must arrange your own medical coverage. Major bridge options include continuation coverage under the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA), individual policies bought through the HealthCare.gov Marketplace, or another employer plan. Another employer plan serves as another possible source; ask the plan administrator about terms and access.

Other health insurance arrangements exist outside these primary paths. You can confirm alternative arrangements directly with a licensed insurance agent. If you calculate overall portfolio milestones alongside medical costs, evaluate your numbers with our [early retirement calculator](/retirement/early-retirement-calculator/).

sections.heading: COBRA Continuation Coverage Rules and Deadlines
sections.body:
COBRA continuation coverage provides temporary health benefits for workers and families who lose employer group coverage, as outlined by the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ebsa/laws-and-regulations/laws/cobra). This law applies to private-sector employers with 20 or more employees. The continuation period lasts usually up to 18 months for qualifying employees and dependents.

You have 60 days to enroll in COBRA coverage. That 60-day election window begins on the date your job-based coverage ends or the date you receive your election notice, whichever is later. You usually pay the entire premium yourself, up to 102% of the plan cost, unless your employer agrees to pay part of it as part of separation.

The additional 2% covers plan administration costs permitted under federal rules. You can review detailed rights on the [U.S. Department of Labor COBRA page](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/health-plans/cobra). If you plan to stop working decades early, see our guide on [how to retire at 40](/guides/how-to-retire-at-40/) to place health care costs in a broader timeline.

sections.heading: Marketplace Coverage and Special Enrollment Periods
sections.body:
You may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period on [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage-outside-open-enrollment/special-enrollment-period/) if you lost qualifying health coverage in the past 60 days or expect to lose it in the next 60 days. Retirement itself is not listed as a qualifying life event on HealthCare.gov. Instead, the loss of your job-based health benefits serves as the qualifying change.

Voluntarily dropping COBRA coverage before it expires does not qualify you for a Special Enrollment Period. Choosing to stop paying your COBRA premiums also does not qualify you for that enrollment window. When your COBRA coverage period ends, you have a 60-day window to enroll in a Marketplace policy.

Special enrollment can also occur based on estimated household income according to HealthCare.gov guidelines. Ask HealthCare.gov how premium tax credits and your income estimate apply to you. Because Roth conversions and portfolio withdrawals can alter reported taxable earnings, review our guide on the [Roth conversion ladder](/guides/roth-conversion-ladder/) and consult a certified public accountant (CPA).

sections.heading: Tradeoffs Across Early Retirement Health Insurance Paths
sections.body:
Evaluating early retirement health insurance requires comparing coverage durations, enrollment deadlines, and premium structures established by federal rules. COBRA provides continuity with your previous group plan but lasts usually up to 18 months. Marketplace plans operate on an annual calendar, with mid-year enrollment permitted only during a 60-day Special Enrollment Period.

Premium costs differ in structure between these two paths. COBRA participants may be required to pay up to 102% of the plan cost directly to the former employer plan administrator. Marketplace premiums vary by policy, and individuals must ask HealthCare.gov how premium tax credits and income estimates apply to their situation.

Another employer plan remains an option. Ask the plan administrator for specific terms, deadlines, and contribution amounts. Missing an election window leaves you without access to that specific pathway until another qualifying event or open enrollment period occurs. To see how variable savings targets absorb multi-year medical premiums, explore our [FIRE calculator](/retirement/fire-calculator/) and our [Coast FIRE guide](/guides/coast-fire-guide/).

sections.heading: When Medicare Coverage Begins at Age 65
sections.body:
Early retirement health insurance ends its primary bridge role once you reach Medicare eligibility at age 65. Your Medicare Initial Enrollment Period begins three months before the month you turn 65 and extends for seven months. For full details on election dates and calendar timelines, consult our guide to [Medicare enrollment periods](/guides/medicare-enrollment-periods/).

When your coverage begins depends on the month you enroll. The standard 2026 Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 a month. You can review related surcharge tiers and deductibles in our guide to [Medicare Part B and IRMAA costs](/guides/medicare-costs-2026-part-b-premium-irmaa/).

Signing up on time avoids ongoing cost adjustments. If you wait to sign up when you must pay for Part B, you may pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B, and it goes up the longer you wait. For rules regarding how COBRA coverage or other existing policies interact with Medicare enrollment, confirm your situation at [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start).

sections.heading: Checklist for Early Retirement Health Insurance Decisions
sections.body:
Preparing your health coverage transition before leaving your job helps protect against unexpected administrative delays. Ask human resources when your active group medical benefits officially terminate following your final working day. Request written documentation of the COBRA election notice and verify the total monthly premium, including whether it equals 102% of the plan cost.

Contact the plan administrator of any potential alternative employer coverage to determine if you can join. Log into HealthCare.gov to review your local 60-day Special Enrollment Period application process and documentation requirements. Ask a licensed health insurance agent or a financial advisor to help you price the total annual premium cost before finalizing your retirement date.

If you assess overall net worth targets before quitting work, consult our analysis on whether [three million is enough to retire at 40](/guides/is-3-million-enough-to-retire-at-40/). Take the next step by requesting your official COBRA premium quote from your benefits coordinator to establish your baseline early retirement health insurance budget.

The information on this page covers federal health insurance rules and is intended for educational purposes only. It does not constitute legal, tax, investment, or individualized health insurance advice. Rules, eligibility criteria, and premium amounts change, so you should confirm your specific circumstances with a licensed insurance agent, plan administrator, certified public accountant, or financial advisor.

faqs.question: How long can you stay on COBRA after retiring?
faqs.answer: COBRA continuation coverage lasts usually up to 18 months for employees who leave their jobs, according to the U.S. Department of Labor. You have 60 days to elect coverage, starting from the date you receive your election notice or the date your employer coverage ends, whichever is later.

faqs.question: Can you get a Marketplace plan if you retire early?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can enroll in a Marketplace plan through HealthCare.gov. Leaving your job and losing qualifying employer-sponsored health benefits triggers a 60-day Special Enrollment Period before or after the coverage loss. Retirement itself is not listed as a qualifying life event, so your qualification stems from losing qualifying coverage.

faqs.question: Is COBRA cheaper than a Marketplace plan?
faqs.answer: Costs vary depending on your employer plan and your local Marketplace selections. Under COBRA, you usually pay the full premium up to 102% of the plan cost. Marketplace premiums depend on the policy you select, and you should ask HealthCare.gov how premium tax credits and your income estimate apply to you.

faqs.question: What happens to health insurance at 65?
faqs.answer: At age 65, you become eligible for Medicare. Your Medicare Initial Enrollment Period begins three months before the month you turn 65. When your Medicare coverage starts depends on the month you enroll, and standard 2026 Part B coverage carries a premium of $202.90 a month.

faqs.question: Do you need health insurance if you retire early and are healthy?
faqs.answer: Maintaining health coverage protects you from paying the full cost of medical treatments out of pocket if you face an illness or injury. Retiring without coverage leaves you responsible for all medical bills. Reviewing COBRA or Marketplace options before leaving your job ensures you have medical coverage in place before Medicare begins.
